q: A DNA sample is found to contain 30% adenine. Assuming it is double-stranded and obeys Chargaff's rule, the percentage of guanine in the sample is:
A = T = 30%, so A + T = 60%. The remaining 40% is shared equally by G and C, giving G = C = 20%.
Two DNA samples, X and Y, are heated. X denatures at a distinctly higher temperature than Y. The most likely explanation is that:
X has a higher A-T content
X has a higher G-C content
G-C pairs are held by three hydrogen bonds against two for A-T, so a GC-rich DNA needs more thermal energy to separate its strands.
Which single observation most directly rules out a purine-purine base pair in the Watson-Crick model?
The constant 20 A diameter of the helix
Two purines would be too wide and two pyrimidines too narrow to keep the backbone at a uniform 20 A separation, so each pair must be purine + pyrimidine.
In a certain double helix, one complete turn spans 3.4 nm. The number of base pairs between two points 6.8 nm apart along the axis is:
Each turn (3.4 nm) contains 10 bp, so 6.8 nm corresponds to two turns, i.e. 20 base pairs.
If the human diploid genome had 13.2 x 10^9 bp instead of 6.6 x 10^9 bp, the total DNA length per cell would be about:
Length = number of bp x 0.34 nm. Doubling the base pairs doubles the length, giving about 4.4 m instead of 2.2 m.
Which structure would you expect to be MOST accessible to RNA polymerase?
Euchromatin is loosely packed and transcriptionally active, so its DNA is physically accessible to the transcription machinery.
The DNA of a prokaryote is negatively charged and organised into large loops. The proteins holding these loops are:
Histones rich in lysine and arginine
Prokaryotes lack histones; in the nucleoid, positively charged non-histone proteins hold the negatively charged DNA in supercoiled loops.
Arrange in increasing order of DNA content: E. coli, bacteriophage lambda, human haploid genome.
Lambda has 48502 bp, E. coli 4.6 x 10^6 bp and the human haploid genome 3.3 x 10^9 bp.
Which control in Griffith's experiment shows that heat-killed S bacteria are not themselves virulent?
Mice injected with heat-killed S alone survived, proving the dead cells could not cause pneumonia by themselves.
Why could sulphur NOT be used to label phage DNA in the Hershey-Chase experiment?
Sulphur occurs in proteins (cysteine, methionine) but not in DNA, while phosphorus occurs in DNA but not in protein - this is what makes the two labels selective.
In the Meselson-Stahl experiment, which result specifically ruled out CONSERVATIVE replication?
A single hybrid band after one generation
Conservative replication predicts one fully heavy and one fully light band after one generation, never a single intermediate-density band.
Which result specifically ruled out DISPERSIVE replication in the Meselson-Stahl experiment?
Distinct hybrid AND light bands after 40 minutes
Dispersive replication predicts one progressively lighter band, never a distinct pure-light band coexisting with a hybrid band.
If E. coli grown in 15N is shifted to 14N and sampled after three generations (60 minutes), the ratio of hybrid to light DNA will be:
After n generations there are always 2 hybrid molecules and (2^n - 2) light ones. After 3 generations: 2 hybrid and 6 light, i.e. 1 : 3.
dNTPs are described as having a 'dual purpose' in replication because they:
Act as substrate and as the energy source
dNTPs supply the nucleotide to be added and, on hydrolysis of their two terminal phosphates, the energy needed for bond formation.
A template strand reads 3'-TACGGATC-5'. The mRNA transcribed from it will be:
RNA is complementary and antiparallel to the template, with U replacing T: 3'-TACGGATC-5' gives 5'-AUGCCUAG-3'.
A promoter is described as lying 'upstream' of the structural gene. This reference is made with respect to the:
Upstream/downstream are always defined relative to the coding strand (5' to 3'); on the antiparallel template the same position would be downstream.
An mRNA in a eukaryotic cytoplasm is found to be shorter than the DNA segment that produced it. The best explanation is:
Eukaryotic genes are split; introns present in the hnRNA are excised and the exons joined, so the mature mRNA is shorter than the gene.
Which property of the genetic code explains why many single-base substitutions produce no change in the protein?
Because most amino acids have several codons differing mainly at the third base, many third-position substitutions are silent.
An mRNA reads 5'-AUG UUU UUC UUA-3'. The polypeptide formed will be:
AUG = Met (start), UUU = Phe, UUC = Phe, UUA = Leu, giving Met-Phe-Phe-Leu.
A ribozyme is best defined by which example from this chapter?
The 23S rRNA of the bacterial large subunit catalyses peptide bond formation - an RNA acting as an enzyme.
If the 5' UTR of an mRNA is deleted while the coding region is intact, the most likely result is:
The correct protein but inefficient translation
UTRs are not translated but are required for efficient translation, so their loss reduces translational efficiency without changing the coded sequence.
A mutation inactivates the i gene of the lac operon. Which enzyme activity will be present even when lactose is absent?
The i gene codes for the repressor; without a functional repressor the operon cannot be switched off, so all three structural gene products are made constitutively.
Sequencing 3 x 10^9 bases at US $3 per base would cost approximately:
3 x 10^9 bases x $3 = $9 x 10^9, i.e. about US $9 billion - one reason bioinformatics became essential.
Two individuals give identical DNA fingerprints. They are most likely:
Identical (monozygotic) twins arise from one zygote and share the same DNA, so their fingerprints cannot be distinguished.
DNA is a polymer of deoxyribonucleotides; RNA is a polymer of ribonucleotides.
The bond that joins a nitrogenous base to a pentose sugar in a nucleoside is a:
Base + sugar = nucleoside, joined through an N-glycosidic bond.
Nucleotides in a polynucleotide chain are linked by:
The 3'-OH of one sugar links to the 5'-phosphate of the next, forming the 3'-5' phosphodiester backbone.
DNA was first isolated from the nucleus and named 'Nuclein' by:
Meischer identified DNA as an acidic substance present in the nucleus and named it Nuclein.
In a double-stranded DNA sample, if adenine constitutes 20% of the bases, the percentage of cytosine will be:
A = T = 20%, so A + T = 40%. The remaining 60% is shared by G and C equally, so C = 30%.
The number of hydrogen bonds between adenine and thymine is:
A pairs with T through two hydrogen bonds; G pairs with C through three.
The stability of the DNA double helix is contributed to by hydrogen bonding and by:
The plane of one base pair stacks over the next, and this base stacking adds to helix stability.
The central dogma DNA to RNA to Protein was proposed by:
Francis Crick proposed the central dogma of molecular biology.
In a DNA sample, guanine constitutes 30% of the total bases. The percentage of thymine will be:
G = C = 30%, so G + C = 60%. The remaining 40% is shared equally by A and T, so T = 20%.
Chargaff's rule of base equivalence (A = T, G = C) strictly applies to:
Complementary base pairing, on which Chargaff's rule depends, exists only where two strands pair - i.e. double-stranded DNA.
Purines differ structurally from pyrimidines mainly in having:
Purines (adenine, guanine) have a double, fused-ring structure, while pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine, uracil) have a single ring.
If a double-stranded DNA molecule contains 22% thymine, the percentage of guanine in it is:
T = A = 22%, so A + T = 44%. The remaining 56% is shared equally by G and C, so G = 28%.
Deoxyadenosine is the nucleoside formed by the union of adenine with:
Deoxyadenosine = adenine + deoxyribose (via an N-glycosidic bond); adenine + ribose gives adenosine instead.
Reverse transcription, the synthesis of DNA from an RNA template, is also known by the name:
Reverse transcription is also called Teminism, named after Howard Temin, who discovered it along with David Baltimore in 1970.
A DNA/RNA base sequence is considered incomplete, strictly speaking, unless it is accompanied by its:
Since every nucleic acid chain has a definite chemical direction, a sequence written without its indicated 5'->3' or 3'->5' polarity is, strictly speaking, incomplete.
Among the DNA pyrimidine bases, thymine is unique in having:
Three hydrogen bonds in every pairing
A ring structure shared with purines
A methyl group not present in cytosine
Thymine is chemically 5-methyl uracil - it carries a methyl group that cytosine (the other DNA pyrimidine) does not have.
The number of base pairs in the E. coli genome is:
E. coli has 4.6 x 10^6 bp; lambda phage has 48502 bp and the human haploid genome 3.3 x 10^9 bp.
Histones are basic proteins because they are rich in:
Lysine and arginine carry positive charges at cellular pH, allowing histones to bind the negatively charged DNA backbone.
200 bp of DNA on a histone octamer
100 bp of DNA on a histone tetramer
400 bp of DNA on a histone hexamer
1000 bp of DNA on NHC proteins
About 200 bp of DNA winds around a core of eight histone molecules, the histone octamer.
In prokaryotes, DNA is held in large loops in a region called the:
Prokaryotes lack a nucleus; DNA is organised in the nucleoid by positively charged non-histone proteins.
Bacteriophage lambda has a genome of:
Lambda phage contains 48502 base pairs, a standard figure used to show that DNA length is a species characteristic.
The human haploid genome (3.3 x 10^9 bp) is approximately how many times larger than the E. coli genome (4.6 x 10^6 bp)?
3.3 x 10^9 / 4.6 x 10^6 is approximately 717, so the human haploid genome is roughly 700 times larger than that of E. coli.
Euchromatin and heterochromatin are distinguished under the light microscope mainly on the basis of:
Euchromatin stains lightly (loosely packed), while heterochromatin stains darkly (densely packed) - a difference visible directly under the light microscope.
A defining structural difference relevant to DNA packaging between a prokaryotic and a eukaryotic cell is that a prokaryote lacks a:
Prokaryotes lack a well-defined, membrane-bound nucleus; their DNA is scattered in the cytoplasm in a region called the nucleoid, unlike the membrane-bound nucleus of…
If a chromatin fibre contains 50 nucleosomes in series, and each nucleosome wraps about 200 bp of DNA, the fibre contains approximately:
50 nucleosomes x 200 bp each = 10000 bp = 10 kb.
According to the NCERT text, the length of DNA (its number of nucleotide/base pairs) is described as:
A universal constant, identical in all species
A characteristic feature of the organism
Always exactly 2.2 metres in every cell
Length is described as a characteristic feature of the organism, illustrated by the very different genome sizes of phi-X174, lambda phage, E. coli and humans.
Griffith's transformation experiment was performed on:
Frederick Griffith (1928) used the S and R strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae in mice.
In Griffith's experiment, mice died when injected with:
Live R strain plus heat-killed S strain
The mixture killed the mice, and live S bacteria were recovered - demonstrating transformation of R into S.
The virulence of the S strain of Streptococcus pneumoniae is attributed to its:
The mucous polysaccharide coat protects the S strain from host defences, making it virulent.
Avery, MacLeod and McCarty identified the transforming principle as DNA because transformation was abolished by:
Only DNase inhibited transformation; proteases and RNases had no effect.
In the Hershey-Chase experiment, 32P was used to label:
Phosphorus occurs in DNA but not protein, so 32P selectively labels the phage DNA.
After blending and centrifugation, radioactivity was found inside the bacterial cells in the case of phages labelled with:
Only DNA (32P) entered the bacterium; the 35S-labelled protein coats remained outside.
RNA is the genetic material in:
TMV and Qbeta bacteriophage are the standard examples of viruses with RNA genomes.
RNA is less stable than DNA mainly because of:
Presence of the 2'-OH group at every nucleotide
The reactive 2'-OH group makes RNA labile and easily degradable.
Bacteriophages, used by Hershey and Chase in their experiment, are viruses that specifically infect:
Bacteriophages are viruses that infect bacteria; Hershey and Chase used them to determine whether protein or DNA is the genetic material.
The scientist(s) who first showed that purified DNA alone, isolated from heat-killed S bacteria, could transform live R bacteria into S bacteria were:
Avery, MacLeod and McCarty (1933-44) purified DNA, protein and RNA separately and showed that DNA alone caused transformation.
Unlike DNA, RNA can itself act as a biocatalyst; this catalytic form of RNA is called a:
RNA molecules that act as biocatalysts, capable of catalysing biochemical reactions, are called ribozymes - this catalytic ability makes RNA more chemically reactive…
Semi-conservative DNA replication was first proposed by:
Watson and Crick proposed it in 1953, immediately after proposing the double helix; Meselson and Stahl proved it in 1958.
Meselson and Stahl grew E. coli in a medium whose nitrogen source was:
15NH4Cl provided the heavy nitrogen isotope that made the DNA heavy.
Heavy and light DNA in the Meselson-Stahl experiment were separated by:
15N is not radioactive, so the DNAs can only be distinguished by density in a CsCl gradient.
In the Meselson-Stahl experiment, DNA extracted after 40 minutes (two generations) showed:
Equal amounts of hybrid and light DNA
After one generation all DNA was hybrid; after two generations hybrid and light DNA were present in equal amounts.
Taylor and colleagues (1958) demonstrated semi-conservative replication of chromosomes using:
Radioactive thymidine in Vicia faba showed that chromosomal DNA also replicates semi-conservatively.
The energy for DNA polymerisation comes from:
dNTPs serve a dual purpose - substrate and energy source, through hydrolysis of their terminal phosphates.
DNA polymerase catalyses polymerisation only in the direction:
Nucleotides can only be added to a free 3'-OH end, so synthesis is strictly 5' to 3'.
DNA ligase seals the nicks between adjacent Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand.
E. coli replicates its 4.6 x 10^6 bp genome in 38 minutes. The average rate of polymerisation is about:
4.6 x 10^6 bp over 2280 seconds gives approximately 2000 base pairs per second.
DNA replication in a eukaryotic cell occurs in the:
Replication is confined to the S (synthesis) phase of interphase.
If DNA polymerase works at about 2000 bp/sec, the time taken to replicate a 60000 bp plasmid from a single origin is approximately:
DNA polymerase, the main enzyme of replication, is more fully described as a:
DNA polymerase uses a DNA template to synthesise a new DNA strand, so it is fully described as a DNA-dependent DNA polymerase.
Using the rate of 2000 bp/sec, the time needed to replicate a 240000 bp region of DNA continuously is:
The role of dNTPs as an energy source during DNA replication arises from hydrolysis of:
All three phosphates into separate free ions
dNTPs provide energy for polymerisation through the hydrolysis of their two terminal phosphates.
If a single replication fork synthesises DNA continuously at 2000 bp/sec for 5 minutes, the length of DNA synthesised by that fork is approximately:
2000 bp/sec x 300 sec (5 minutes) = 6 x 10^5 bp.
A transcription unit is the structural gene flanked by a promoter and a terminator.
The DNA strand that serves as template during transcription has the polarity:
RNA polymerase works only 5' to 3', so it must read a template running 3' to 5'.
A segment of DNA coding for a single polypeptide is called a:
A cistron is a structural gene segment carrying the code for one polypeptide.
Split genes containing introns are characteristic of:
Eukaryotic structural genes are mostly monocistronic and split; prokaryotic genes are mostly polycistronic.
In prokaryotes, the initiation factor of transcription is:
Sigma factor alters RNA polymerase specificity for initiation; rho factor is required for termination.
In eukaryotes, hnRNA (the precursor of mRNA) is transcribed by:
Pol I transcribes 28S, 18S and 5.8S rRNA; Pol II transcribes hnRNA; Pol III transcribes tRNA, 5S rRNA and snRNA.
Capping of hnRNA involves the addition of:
A poly-U tail at the 5' end
Methyl guanosine triphosphate at the 5' end
Capping is at the 5' end with methyl guanosine triphosphate; tailing at the 3' end adds 200-300 adenylate residues.
Given a template strand reading 3'-ATGCATGC-5', the mRNA transcribed from it will read:
Reading the template 3' to 5' (A,T,G,C,A,T,G,C) and pairing complementarily (A-U, T-A, G-C, C-G) gives the mRNA, read 5' to 3', as UACGUACG.
RNA polymerase I in the eukaryotic nucleus transcribes:
RNA polymerase I transcribes the larger rRNAs (28S, 18S and 5.8S); polymerase II transcribes hnRNA; polymerase III transcribes tRNA, 5S rRNA and snRNA.
The three sequential steps of transcription are:
Transcription proceeds through initiation (RNA polymerase binds the promoter), elongation (the RNA chain is polymerised) and termination (the polymerase releases the…
If a coding strand reads 5'-ATGGCTTAC-3', the mRNA transcribed from the complementary template strand will read:
The coding strand's sequence is identical to the mRNA except that RNA has uracil instead of thymine, so 5'-ATGGCTTAC-3' becomes 5'-AUGGCUUAC-3'.
hnRNA, before it undergoes processing, contains:
The primary transcript hnRNA contains both exons and introns and is non-functional until introns are removed by splicing.
Structural genes, cistrons and regulatory genes are all components found within a:
A transcription unit (in prokaryotes, an operon) consists of structural genes (cistrons) flanked by regulatory elements such as the promoter and terminator, along…
A DNA sequence coding for a tRNA or rRNA molecule, even though it produces no polypeptide, is still called a:
A gene is defined as the functional unit of inheritance, and this definition also covers DNA sequences coding for tRNA or rRNA molecules, not just polypeptide-coding…
The genetic code was proposed to be a triplet on mathematical grounds by:
Gamow reasoned that 4^3 = 64 combinations are needed to code 20 amino acids, since 4^2 = 16 is too few.
Cell-free systems for protein synthesis, which helped decipher the code, were developed by:
Nirenberg's cell-free system allowed synthetic RNAs to be translated so codons could be assigned to amino acids.
Of the 64 codons, the number that code for amino acids is:
61 codons specify amino acids and 3 (UAA, UAG, UGA) act as stop codons.
The codon AUG has dual function because it:
Acts as start codon and codes for methionine
Acts as both start and stop codon
AUG initiates translation and also specifies methionine wherever it occurs internally.
UAA, UAG and UGA are also known as:
They specify no amino acid; their nicknames are ochre (UAA), amber (UAG) and opal (UGA).
In human mitochondria, an exception to the universality of the genetic code is that UGA codes for:
In human mitochondria UGA codes for tryptophan, AGA/AGG act as stop signals, and AUA codes for methionine.
Insertion of a single base pair in a coding sequence causes a:
Because codons are read in fixed triplets, insertion or deletion of one base shifts the reading frame downstream.
In sickle-cell anaemia, glutamic acid is replaced by which amino acid in the beta-globin chain?
The change CTC to CAC substitutes valine for glutamic acid - a classic point mutation.
There are no tRNA molecules corresponding to:
No anticodon pairs with UAA, UAG or UGA; a release factor binds instead and terminates translation.
Severo Ochoa's enzyme, which polymerises RNA with defined sequences in a template-independent manner, is called:
Polynucleotide phosphorylase, Ochoa's enzyme, polymerised RNA of defined sequences without needing a template, contributing to deciphering the genetic code.
Using the standard codon table, the codon GAA specifies the amino acid:
GAA and GAG both code for glutamic acid (Glu) in the standard codon table.
Using the standard codon table, the codon UGG specifies the amino acid:
UGG codes for tryptophan (Trp); UGU and UGC code for cysteine, and UGA is a stop codon.
Of the 64 possible codons, the fraction that are stop (nonsense) codons is:
Only 3 of the 64 codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) are stop codons; the remaining 61 code for amino acids.
The initiator tRNA carries the amino acid:
The initiator tRNA, whose anticodon UAC pairs with the AUG start codon, carries methionine.
Linking an activated amino acid to its specific tRNA is called:
Amino acids are first activated using ATP and then charged onto their corresponding tRNA.
Peptide bond formation in bacterial ribosomes is catalysed by:
The 23S rRNA of the large subunit is the catalyst - an RNA enzyme, or ribozyme.
A release factor binds the stop codon
A release factor recognises the stop codon and releases the completed polypeptide.
The lac operon was elucidated in 1961 by:
Francois Jacob (geneticist) and Jacques Monod (biochemist) worked out the lac operon.
In the lac operon, beta-galactosidase is coded by the:
z codes beta-galactosidase, y codes permease, a codes transacetylase and i codes the repressor.
The lac operon repressor protein is coded by the:
The i (inhibitor) gene is a regulatory gene whose product binds the operator.
In the absence of lactose, transcription of the lac operon is blocked because:
The repressor binds the operator region
The repressor occupies the operator and prevents RNA polymerase from transcribing z, y and a - negative regulation.
The inducer of the lac operon is:
Lactose, or its metabolite allolactose, inactivates the repressor and switches the operon on.
The trp operon of E. coli is an example of a:
Inducible operon in a catabolic pathway
Repressible operon in an anabolic pathway
The trp operon is normally on and is switched off when tryptophan accumulates - feedback repression in an anabolic pathway.
The lac operon system was worked out by a geneticist and a biochemist, respectively named:
Francois Jacob, a geneticist, and Jacques Monod, a biochemist, together worked out the lac operon as a transcriptionally regulated system.
In the trp operon, the region between the operator and structural gene E that helps regulate the attenuator is called the:
The leader sequence (L) lies between the operator and structural gene E and controls the attenuator.
Since an operon places multiple structural genes under one promoter, the single mRNA transcribed from it is described as:
Because an operon's structural genes (like z, y and a of the lac operon) are transcribed together as one mRNA carrying the code for multiple polypeptides, that mRNA…
The Human Genome Project was a project spanning:
The HGP was launched in 1990 and completed in 2003, a 13-year mega project.
US Department of Energy and NIH
The US Department of Energy and the National Institutes of Health coordinated it; the Wellcome Trust (UK) joined later.
The estimated number of genes in the human genome is about:
The HGP estimated about 30000 genes, far fewer than had been expected.
The largest known human gene is:
Dystrophin spans 2.4 million bases; an average human gene is about 3000 bases.
The proportion of the human genome that codes for proteins is:
Less than 2% of the genome is protein-coding; much of the rest consists of repetitive sequences.
The human chromosome with the fewest genes is:
The Y chromosome carries the fewest genes (231); chromosome 1 carries the most (2968).
SNPs in the human genome occur at approximately:
Single nucleotide polymorphisms at about 1.4 million sites help explain disease and trace evolutionary history.
The two methods used in the HGP to identify genes were:
Expressed Sequence Tags and sequence annotation
ESTs target only expressed regions; sequence annotation sequences the whole genome and then assigns function.
The vectors used to clone genomic fragments during the HGP were:
Bacterial and yeast artificial chromosomes were used, with bacteria and yeast as hosts.
The sequence data generated by the Human Genome Project would require approximately how many books of 1000 pages each, just for one human genome?
The sequence data generated by the HGP would require about 3300 books of 1000 pages each just for one human genome, illustrating the enormous scale of data that led…
What percentage of base sequences is identical between any two human beings?
99.9% is identical; the remaining 0.1% underlies individual uniqueness and DNA fingerprinting.
DNA fingerprinting was initially developed by:
Alec Jeffreys developed the technique, using VNTRs as probes.
In DNA fingerprinting, DNA fragments separated by electrophoresis are transferred to a nylon membrane by:
Southern blotting immobilises DNA fragments on nylon or nitrocellulose for hybridisation with a probe.
VNTRs used as probes in DNA fingerprinting vary in size from:
Because VNTRs vary from 0.1 to 20 kb, bands of many different sizes appear on the autoradiogram.
DNA fingerprints are identical only in:
Monozygotic twins arise from one zygote and share the same DNA, so their fingerprints cannot be distinguished.
Drosophila melanogaster's whole genome was sequenced in the year:
The fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster's whole genome was sequenced in the year 2000, alongside the ongoing HGP.
The Wellcome Trust, which joined the coordination of the Human Genome Project at a later stage, is based in:
The HGP was coordinated by the US Department of Energy and NIH, later joined by the Wellcome Trust, a UK-based organisation.
If A = 30% in a DNA, G is:
Sulphur is in protein, not DNA.
Okazaki fragments are formed on the:
Discontinuous synthesis on the lagging strand.
I → rRNA, II → hnRNA, III → tRNA, 5S rRNA, snRNA.
In bacteria, peptidyl transferase activity is due to:
The histone octamer contains two each of:
H1 is the linker histone, not in the octamer.
